thresholds.spillway_label: Overflow spillway crest / top of flood pool
thresholds.record_high_note: LCRA historic high, daily 8 a.m. reading
thresholds.record_low_note: LCRA historic low, daily 8 a.m. reading

flood_stage_note: The 700 ft line is included because it was requested as a reference. It sits in LCRA's flood pool (681–714 ft) and is not a verified official LCRA “flood stage.” LCRA uses “flood stage” as an NWS / local term, not as a 700 ft gauge at Mansfield Dam. Official marked levels are conservation / full pool at 681 ft and the overflow spillway / top of flood pool at 714 ft.

climatology.note: Typical seasonal levels use TWDB daily averages from 1943-01-01 through 2026-11-20. 1940–1941 filling years are excluded because the reservoir was still coming into service and TWDB values fall below LCRA's official 1951 record low (614.18 ft). 1942 is also set aside: that year has only 101 sparse month-end values, not a continuous daily record. Each calendar month's mean, median, and 10th/90th percentiles are computed from that month's yearly mean elevation, so each year counts equally.

same_date_note: TWDB daily average elevation on November 20 of each year. Today's live LCRA reading is 681.43 ft; the TWDB figure for today is a daily average and may differ, especially while the lake is rising or falling quickly.

rises_2026.title: November 9–10, 2026 (still rising)
rises_2026.lead: A rise still in progress as LCRA moves Llano River floodwaters into Lake Travis.
rises_2026.attribution: Rain event — not attributed to a named tropical storm. LCRA's flood page and CBS Austin reported heavy rain west of the Highland Lakes and high flows on the Llano River. LCRA opened floodgates at Wirtz and Starcke dams to pass that water downstream into Lake Travis, and projected the lake would rise to 680–681 ft over the next 24–48 hours. No floodgate operations were expected at Mansfield Dam.

sources.name: CBS Austin, November 10, 2026: Wirtz and Starcke gates, Llano floodwaters

rises_2026.series_source: LCRA Hydromet 5-minute readings at Mansfield Dam (site 3963)

rises_2026.title: October 1–7, 2026
rises_2026.lead: Most of this rise happened in the first three days; the lake then crept to a crest on October 7.
rises_2026.attribution: Remnants of Hurricane Polo interacting with a cold front. Texas Public Radio, on October 1, reported that the National Weather Service issued flash flood warnings for portions of Bandera, Gillespie, Kerr, and Real counties as Polo's remnants interacted with a cold front, and that a flood warning was in effect for the Llano River at Llano. The next morning, KUT reported that LCRA had opened floodgates at Wirtz and Starcke dams to pass Llano River floodwaters downstream into Lake Travis.

sources.name: Texas Public Radio, October 1, 2026: Polo remnants and a cold front
KUT, October 2, 2026: Wirtz and Starcke floodgates, water into Lake Travis

rises_2026.series_source: LCRA Hydromet 5-minute readings at Mansfield Dam (site 3963)

rises_2026.title: July 16–19, 2026
rises_2026.lead: The year's largest rise. The lake climbed into its flood pool, and LCRA opened floodgates at Mansfield Dam for the first time since 2019.
rises_2026.attribution: Hill Country rain event — not attributed to a named tropical storm. LCRA reported that storms over the preceding days brought 1–4 inches of rain to much of the region, with some areas near Junction and Fredericksburg receiving as much as a foot, sending runoff toward Lake Travis. Axios, using LCRA data, reported the lake climbed roughly 13 feet between July 16 and July 19. Tropical Storm Bertha did not form until July 20, after this rise had crested.

sources.name: LCRA, July 17, 2026: floodgate operations at Mansfield Dam
Axios Austin, July 20, 2026: Charted: Lake Travis rises

rises_2026.series_source: LCRA Hydromet 5-minute readings at Mansfield Dam (site 3963)

rises_2026.title: June 14–16, 2026
rises_2026.lead: A short, sharp bump during a night of flash flooding in the Austin area.
rises_2026.attribution: Rain event — not attributed to a named tropical storm. KUT reported flash flooding, water rescues, and 3–4 inches of rain in parts of Travis County from midnight to early afternoon on June 15, with NWS flash flood warnings for Travis, Hays, and Williamson counties. LCRA opened a floodgate at Tom Miller Dam that morning. Tropical Storm Arthur formed on June 17 near the Texas coast, after this rise; no source reviewed here ties the Lake Travis rise to Arthur, so it is not named as the cause.
rises_2026.series_source: LCRA Hydromet 5-minute readings at Mansfield Dam (site 3963)

rises_2026.title: May 21–28, 2026
rises_2026.lead: A late-May rise in two pulses, steepest overnight May 26–27 when LCRA opened a floodgate at Starcke Dam.
rises_2026.attribution: Rain event (severe thunderstorms) — not attributed to a named tropical storm. LCRA warned on May 26 of a line of strong to severe storms and widespread soaking rain (1–3 inches, isolated pockets up to 5 inches) under an NWS Flood Watch. The Daily Trib reported that storms that evening washed out roads in the Highland Lakes area and that LCRA opened a Starcke Dam floodgate overnight to pass runoff into Lake Travis. The lake had already begun rising on May 20–23 and continued a slow creep to 670.00 ft early on June 1.

sources.name: Daily Trib, May 27, 2026: severe rainfall in the Highland Lakes

rises_2026.series_source: LCRA Hydromet 5-minute readings at Mansfield Dam (site 3963)

rises_note: A sharp rise is a gain of more than 1 foot over a few days. Elevations, rates, and peak 24-hour rises for 2026 come from LCRA Hydromet 5-minute readings (available back to mid-May 2026). A storm is named only when a cited NWS, LCRA, or news source ties that storm or its remnants to the rain or river flows that raised Lake Travis; otherwise the event is called a rain event.

historical_rises.title: July 2025 Hill Country flood
historical_rises.note: LCRA reported that from 7 a.m. Friday, July 4, through July 17, 2025, Lake Travis rose more than 36 feet. TWDB daily averages show 637.78 ft on July 4 and 673.70 ft on July 17. A second pulse followed mid-month. This was a Hill Country rain/flood event, not used here as a named-storm attribution.

source.name: TWDB daily history for Lake Travis

historical_rises.title: October 2018
historical_rises.note: The largest well-documented rise in the modern daily record used here: TWDB daily averages show the lake going from 658.77 ft on October 7 to 704.28 ft on October 20, including a 19.58 ft jump from October 16 to 17.

source.name: LCRA dams and lakes (official record high)

historical_rises.title: December 1991 (official record high)
historical_rises.note: LCRA's official historic high is 710.44 ft msl on December 25, 1991, from a daily 8 a.m. reading. TWDB daily averages peak at 710.31 ft on December 26 (710.16 ft on December 25). The two sources use different methods; the official record is LCRA's.

historical_note: Historical comparisons use TWDB daily averages, which can differ from LCRA instantaneous or 8 a.m. readings. The September 1952 TWDB series shows an extremely large rise, including a one-day jump of about 56 ft on September 12, which may include a gap or catch-up in the daily record; it is not used as a headline comparison.

caveats: Every elevation on this page comes from published LCRA or TWDB data. Nothing is interpolated as a fake reading.
Times are America/Chicago (Central Time), labeled CST or CDT.
1-/7-/30-day changes use the LCRA 5-minute series at the same time of day, not the midnight values in LakeLevelsRR.csv.
LCRA percent full and storage can lag the latest 5-minute elevation by a few minutes.
TWDB daily averages and LCRA instantaneous or 8 a.m. readings can differ, especially on fast-changing days. Percent-full methods also differ.
The Hydromet historic API returns about 179 days of 5-minute data. Longer charts use TWDB daily values (monthly means for the all-time view).
